entries.title: Two thousand baths, or three thousand?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 7:26 says Solomon's bronze Sea held two thousand baths. 2 Chronicles 4:5 says three thousand. The CSB emends Chronicles to match Kings.
entries.plain: The real question: how much did the great basin hold, and why do the two books differ? **One brochure says the tank holds 2,000 gallons, and the other says 3,000.** A misprint, or two different ways of measuring?
entries.claim: 1 Kings 7:26 says the cast bronze Sea in front of the temple contained two thousand baths. 2 Chronicles 4:5 says it received and held three thousand.
entries.diag: The ESV Study Bible, on 2 Chronicles 4:2-6, notes that 1 Kings 7:26 reads two thousand and says the difference may be due to a copyist's error. The CSB converts both verses to gallons and prints the same figure, about eleven thousand gallons, at both places; its textual note on 2 Chronicles 4:5 marks the text as emended from the Hebrew 3,000 baths, with a reference to 1 Kings 7:26.
entries.kjv: And the thickness of it was an handbreadth, and the brim of it like the work of the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies; and it received and held three thousand baths.
entries.kjvRole: the King James follows the Hebrew three thousand
entries.kjvNote: 1 Kings 7:26 in the same translation ends: "it contained two thousand baths."
entries.skeptic: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible asks "What was the volume of the molten sea?" and sets 2,000 against 3,000, quoting the New Oxford Annotated Bible's note on 2 Chronicles 4:5. At full strength: these are measurements of a single bronze object the writers could have seen or read about, and they differ by half.
entries.harm: MacArthur does not call it a copying error. He reconciles the figures by having Chronicles count the water the basin held plus the supply needed to keep it flowing as a fountain. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible takes each figure as written, about 12,000 gallons at 1 Kings 7:26 and about 18,000 at 2 Chronicles 4:5, without addressing the difference.
entries.cost: The harmonizers are split, and the ESV Study Bible says only that the difference may be a copyist's error. The copying diagnosis is the leading one in the sources read here, not a settled one. MacArthur's fountain reading has no support in the text quoted here; that is an observation made here.
entries.not: **Not a claim that the Chronicler was careless.** The diagnosis is that the error, if it is one, came in copying.

entries.title: Seventeen hundred horsemen, or seven thousand?
entries.summary: The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 says David took 1,700 horsemen. 1 Chronicles 18:4 says 1,000 chariots and 7,000 horsemen. The Septuagint and a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel read with Chronicles.
entries.plain: The real question: what did David capture, and why do the two lists differ? **The receipt says 1,700 chairs, and the order form says 1,000 tables and 7,000 chairs.** Did the store lose part of a line?
entries.claim: 2 Samuel 8:4 says David took from Hadadezer 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers. 1 Chronicles 18:4 says 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers.
entries.diag: The ESV prints 1,700 horsemen at 2 Samuel 8:4, and the ESV Study Bible says the Septuagint agrees with Chronicles; one possible explanation is that someone miscopied Samuel and the Septuagint, with Chronicles, keeps the true reading. The CSB's textual note says the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls read 1,000 chariots and 7,000 horsemen. MacArthur calls 1,700 a copyist's error. This is the number entry with the widest outside support: a Greek translation and a Hebrew scroll of Samuel side with Chronicles.
entries.kjv: And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen:
entries.kjvRole: the King James reads a thousand chariots and seven hundred horsemen
entries.kjvNote: The King James figures are neither the Hebrew 1,700 horsemen nor Chronicles' 7,000. Reading them as the translators' way of splitting 1,700 into chariots and horsemen is an inference drawn here. 1 Chronicles 18:4 in the same translation: "And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen".
entries.skeptic: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible asks "How many horsemen did David take?" and, quoting the King James, sets seven hundred horsemen against seven thousand. At full strength: even the translation that tried to bring the two verses together leaves them disagreeing.
entries.harm: The harmonizing case is the copying case: Samuel lost part of the line, and Chronicles, the Septuagint and the Qumran text preserve it. MacArthur says the 7,000 of Chronicles is the preferable reading.
entries.cost: The ESV Study Bible says there is not enough information to account for the difference, so even its preferred explanation is offered as possible, not shown. The CSB note gives the Dead Sea Scrolls without naming the scroll, and no scroll is named here.
entries.not: **Not a claim that David's victory is in doubt.** Both books report the same campaign; the dispute is over one line of the tally.

entries.title: Baasha's war after Baasha's death
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles 16:1 has Baasha of Israel attack Judah in Asa's thirty-sixth year. By the dates in 1 Kings, Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth.
entries.plain: The real question: did a dead king start a war, or is a date wrong? **The plaque says the founder opened the new wing in 1990, and his gravestone says he died in 1980.** A typo, or a different way of counting?
entries.claim: 2 Chronicles 16:1 says that in the thirty-sixth year of Asa, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah and built Ramah. 1 Kings 16:8 says Baasha's son Elah began to reign in Asa's twenty-sixth year, so Baasha was by then dead.
entries.diag: The ESV Study Bible says Baasha had been dead ten years by the date given and offers a copying error as one possible explanation. Letters of the Hebrew alphabet were used as numerals, and a scribe might have confused yod, for 10, with lamedh, for 30, letters that looked more alike in early handwriting than in modern type. The original would then be Asa's sixteenth year. It says the same confusion may affect 2 Chronicles 15:19.
entries.kjv: In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah, to the intent that he might let none go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.
entries.kjvRole: the King James reads the thirty-sixth year
entries.kjvNote: 1 Kings 16:8 in the same translation: "In the twenty and sixth year of Asa king of Judah began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah, two years."
entries.skeptic: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible sets 1 Kings 16:6-8, Baasha's death in Asa's twenty-sixth year, against 2 Chronicles 16:1, and remarks that if both are true, then "Baasha fought with Judah ten years after his death!"
entries.harm: MacArthur avoids any error. He reads the thirty-sixth year as counted from the division of the kingdom, not from Asa's accession, which puts the war in Asa's sixteenth year, and says that manner of reckoning was used in the royal annals the Chronicler drew on.
entries.cost: Two rival explanations land on the same year, Asa's sixteenth. The ESV Study Bible's copying explanation is offered as one possibility; MacArthur's change of starting point needs no error but assumes a reckoning the verse does not state. Filing this as a copying error follows the ESV Study Bible and is the less certain of the two classifications on this desk's terms.
entries.not: **Not a claim that Kings and Chronicles disagree about who ruled when.** Both explanations keep their regnal lists in agreement.

entries.title: Saul was one year old
entries.summary: The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 says Saul was a year old when he became king and reigned two years. Paul says he reigned forty. The numbers in the Hebrew appear to be damaged.
entries.plain: The real question: how long did Saul reign, and what happened to the verse? **The old ledger says he took over the shop at age one and ran it for two years, and his son says he ran it for forty.** Is the ledger wrong, or is a number missing?
entries.claim: Read literally, the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 says Saul was one year old when he became king and reigned two years over Israel. Paul, in Acts 13:21, says God gave Israel Saul for forty years.
entries.diag: The ESV footnote gives the Hebrew as Saul was one year old when he became king, and he reigned two years over Israel, and says some Greek manuscripts give his age as thirty. The ESV Study Bible says numbers giving Saul's age and the length of his reign may have been lost from the text very early, and that most Septuagint manuscripts lack the verse entirely. The CSB's textual notes say some Septuagint manuscripts omit the verse and that the CSB's figure for the length of the reign is an emendation of the Hebrew two years. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says the numerals thirty and forty in the NIV do not appear in the Hebrew, and that omitted numerals occur in other ancient Near Eastern texts, including the Sumerian King List and the Babylonian Chronicles.
entries.kjv: Saul reigned one year; and when he had reigned two years over Israel,
entries.kjvRole: the King James makes it a reign, not an age
entries.kjvNote: The King James sidesteps the age and gives no total. Acts 13:21 in the same translation: "God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years."
entries.skeptic: No source read for this build states this one, so it is given as it circulates: the Hebrew says Saul was a year old and reigned two years, Paul says forty, and translators hide the problem by inserting numbers the Hebrew does not have. At full strength: modern versions print figures no Hebrew manuscript contains.
entries.harm: The CSB Study Bible says manuscripts differ on the length of the reign and that, comparing them with Acts 13:21 as a round number, forty-two years is most likely. MacArthur says the original numbers have not been preserved and suggests Saul was perhaps thirty-one. The ESV prints a reading that makes sense of the Hebrew as it stands, Saul lived for one year and then became king, and its study note mentions, as only a speculative possibility, a comment on Saul's immaturity. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible suggests the year and two years may count from Saul's anointing and to his rejection.
entries.cost: Even granting a lost numeral, no one has the original. Translations that print thirty and forty-two are reconstructing. The NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible says Saul's age at accession must remain open and estimates a reign of about twenty or twenty-two years, which does not match Paul's forty; it notes that Josephus gives twenty in one place, and on Acts 13:21 that Paul's figure fits one line of Jewish tradition. So the diagnosis explains the Hebrew. It leaves the length of the reign unsettled.
entries.not: **Not a claim that the Hebrew says Saul was a baby.** Every source read takes the text as damaged or idiomatic, not as a statement about an infant king.
